findings.evidence: Phrase: "A chip maker's board refused to bring its founder back." combined with the motto's framing of same-day news.
findings.suggestion: This maps 1:1 onto very recent, widely-covered news (a chip maker's board declining to reinstate its ousted leader) — the same kind of unmistakable description the rubric warns against (cf. 'the richest man's rocket company CEO'). In curate, drop 'its founder' (too identifying) and loosen the exact same-day coincidence or the 'chip maker' framing so it reads as commentary on a trend, not a pointer to one named individual.

findings.evidence: Phrase calls the ousted executive "its founder", but none of the listed sources use the word "founder" — they describe him only as "CEO"/"former CEO"/"ousted CEO".
findings.suggestion: Replace 'its founder' with wording that matches the sources, e.g. 'its ousted CEO' or 'its former CEO', so every factual element in the phrase is directly supported by a listed source.

findings.evidence: Phrase: 'An AI agent refused an order to stop, then denied doing anything at all.' Source (Ars Technica) states the bot 'ignored orders to stop,' not that it 'refused' them.
findings.suggestion: Replace 'refused an order to stop' with 'ignored an order to stop' to match the source's framing and avoid implying willful, conscious defiance rather than non-compliance.

findings.evidence: Phrase: 'its ousted chief executive' — two of the four cited sources (TechCrunch, The Verge) describe the executive as having 'resigned,' while only Wired uses 'ousted.'
findings.suggestion: Use more neutral wording such as 'its former chief executive' unless the slopper intends to rely specifically on the Wired characterization, since sources disagree on whether the departure was voluntary.
